title: Pastors and money
hookLine: a preacher's sneakers go viral; the New Testament has more to say about church money than people expect

lines: IS THIS WHERE MY TITHE GOES?
cards: A photo goes around online. A preacher on a big stage, mid-sermon, arms raised. Someone has circled his sneakers in red and added a price: a few thousand dollars.
Underneath, the comments pile up. Is this where my tithe goes? There are whole accounts built around pictures like that, and some people quietly stop giving because of them.
It's a fair question, and an old one. The first Christians asked it too, and the New Testament answers it more directly than people expect. Today's word is an old one for money made the wrong way.

teach.b: It means gain or profit, from the Latin lucrum, and the King James Bible usually puts a word in front of it: filthy lucre.

Here's a letter written to church leaders, in that translation: "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind."
The Greek behind it means for shameful gain. So the warning about leaders in it for the money isn't a modern cynic's idea. It's in the Bible.

Now the other side. Paul says plainly that "they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Paying a pastor isn't a scandal, and some pastors work a second job so a small church can afford them.
Paul himself often worked with his hands, making tents, so no one could say he preached for money.
Then the part for anyone who has wondered where their gift goes. Paul was carrying a large collection from the churches to the poor in Jerusalem, and he refused to handle it alone.
Others, chosen by the churches, traveled with it.

teach.h: HONEST IN THE SIGHT OF ALL.
teach.b: His reason, in the King James words: "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men." Honest before God, and visible to everyone else.

That's still the shape many churches aim for: open books, a board that sets the pastor's pay, outside checks. Some publish their budgets for anyone to read. Asking where the money goes isn't a lack of faith.

how: Many churches publish annual budgets, have an elected board or council set clergy pay, and use outside audits; members are generally free to ask how gifts are spent.

games.q: you're Paul. churches have trusted you with a large gift for the poor in Jerusalem. it's a long road, and you know you're honest. what do you do?
o: carry it alone; God knows your heart.
take people chosen by the churches along with you.
spend a little on the trip and explain later.
games.why: Paul wanted it honest "not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men." so others, chosen by the churches, came too.

practice: Bring to mind a place you give to, or once did, or might, a church, a charity, a friend's fundraiser, and notice what you know about where the money goes, and what you don't.

No suspicion needed, and no guilt: just honest eyes, the kind Paul asked for. If you pray, pray for the people who handle gifts, that they'd be faithful; if you don't, simply hold the question kindly.

wordCard.voice: Lucre. Gain or profit, from the Latin lucrum. Church leaders are told to serve not for filthy lucre. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: for shameful gain. one word, which the King James renders for filthy lucre (1 Peter 5:2).

carryVoice: Your line: open books, open hands. Giving freely and asking where it goes belong together. Day one hundred thirty-two.
